# Introduction {#sec-introduction}



## The ageing population and the burden of sarcopenia

**The onset of significant skeletal muscle mass decline in adults represents a complex
temporal process that differs between biological initiation and clinical
manifestation.** While sarcopenia often becomes clinically significant only in the
sixth decade of life, the underlying degenerative processes begin substantially
earlier [@westerstahl2025; @gustafsson2024]. A large-scale cross-sectional analysis
of 50\,332 participants aged 45--84 years reveals continuous decline in fat-free
thigh muscle volume across all age groups [@anderson2025]. This pattern is also
supported by longitudinal evidence [@westerstahl2025].

**Age-related muscle loss results from multiple interconnected physiological and
metabolic changes, including neural degeneration, mitochondrial dysfunction, altered
amino acid metabolism, and impaired muscle protein synthesis.** At the neural level,
healthy older adults experience significant motor unit remodelling, with approximately
40% fewer motor units by age 71 [@piasecki2016]. The progressive loss of muscle mass
is fundamentally driven by the dual mechanisms of muscle fibre atrophy and hypoplasia,
largely resulting from chronic imbalances between muscle protein synthesis (MPS) and
breakdown (MPB) [@wilkinson2018].
